kurals.tamil:
மனைத்தக்க மாண்புடையள் ஆகித்தற் கொண்டான்
வளத்தக்காள் வாழ்க்கைத் துணை.
kurals.transliteration:
Manaith thakka maanbudaiyaL aagith thaR koNdaan,
vaLath thakkaaL vaazhkkaith thuNai.
kurals.meaning: She who possesses the excellences that household life requires, and who orders that life to match the means of the man who married her, is a true life-partner.
kurals.elementary: Imagine two people rowing one boat. It only moves straight if they pull together with the strength each of them actually has — not with strength they wish they had. This kural says a good partner is the one who runs the home well and spends what the family really earns, not what it pretends to earn.
kurals.university: Valluvar opens the chapter with a definition rather than a eulogy, and the definition is startlingly practical: the wife's worth is located in maanbu (moral excellence fitted to the household) plus vaLaththakkaaL — living proportionate to income. Parimelazhagar's classical commentary glosses the "good qualities" as hospitality to ascetics and guests and compassion to the poor, and the "good deeds" as knowing what the household needs, competence in the kitchen, and oppuravu (civic generosity) — so domestic thrift is framed not as miserliness but as the material precondition of ethical generosity established in Chapter 5 (Il-vaazhkkai). The chapter's title is also significant: Valluvar does not call it "manaiviyin maanbu" (the greatness of a wife) but vaazhkkaith-thuNai nalam, "the worth of a life-companion," a word choice Tamil commentators have long read as elevating the wife from an object of the household to its co-agent. Modern feminist readings of the Kural note the asymmetry — the chapter addresses the wife's duties to a far greater extent than the husband's — while also observing that Valluvar's criterion is competence and character rather than birth, beauty, or dowry, which was itself a notable move in the ancient Tamil context.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Manusmriti assigns the wife direct charge of the household economy — the gathering and spending of the family's wealth, the keeping of the house, the preparation of food, and the care of the household goods — making her the manager rather than merely a resident of the home.
hinduism.explanation: Manu 9.11 hands the wife operational control of income and expenditure, precisely the competence Valluvar names.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts define the good wife by her stewardship of what the household actually has.
hinduism.source: Manusmriti 9.11 (trans. G. Bühler, Sacred Books of the East XXV)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a verse whose content matches the kural's economic-stewardship criterion closely, though Manu frames it as the husband 'employing' her.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Who can find a virtuous woman? for her price is far above rubies. The heart of her husband doth safely trust in her, so that he shall have no need of spoil. She will do him good and not evil all the days of her life.”
christianity.explanation: The Proverbs 31 portrait opens by defining the excellent wife economically — her husband needs no plunder because her management supplies the house.
christianity.tie_back: Same criterion as the Kural: worth measured by trustworthy provision within the household's own means.
christianity._accuracy_note: Very close thematic and structural match — both are opening definitions of the worthy wife keyed to household provision.

islam.quote_or_event: “The lady is a guardian and is responsible for her husband's house and his offspring; and so all of you are guardians and are responsible for your wards.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet's 'each of you is a shepherd' hadith assigns the wife a defined stewardship over the home and children, for which she is answerable.
islam.tie_back: Both make the wife the responsible steward of the household, not a dependent within it.
islam.source: Sahih al-Bukhari 5200 (Book of Wedlock/Marriage), narrated by 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar
islam._accuracy_note: Verbatim from the standard sunnah.com English rendering; the stewardship framing matches the kural directly.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And the LORD God said, It is not good that the man should be alone; I will make him an help meet for him.”
judaism.explanation: The foundational Hebrew account of marriage names the wife an ezer kenegdo — a helper corresponding to, and fitted for, the man.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural's 'vaazhkkaith thuNai' — life-helper — stated as a creation principle.
judaism.source: Genesis 2:18 (King James Version); Hebrew ezer kenegdo
judaism._accuracy_note: The Hebrew term for 'helper fitted to him' is almost a lexical twin of the kural's 'life-companion', though Genesis is about marriage's origin rather than household economy.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “She's well-organized in her work. She manages the domestic help. She's not unfaithful. She preserves his earnings. She's deft and tireless in all her duties.”
buddhism.explanation: In the Buddha's lay code, these are the five ways a wife reciprocates a husband who honours her — with 'preserves his earnings' as an explicit duty.
buddhism.tie_back: 'Preserving his earnings' is the Pali equivalent of vaLaththakkaaL — living to the measure of what he brings in.
buddhism.source: Dīgha Nikāya 31, Sigālovāda Sutta (trans. Bhikkhu Sujato, SuttaCentral)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one overlap on the household-management and income-preservation criteria; the Sutta adds reciprocal husbandly duties that Valluvar's chapter does not.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Odyssey, Queen Arete of the Phaeacians is so honoured by her husband Alcinous and by the people that Odysseus is told to appeal to her knees first, because she settles disputes even among men and her goodwill decides whether he reaches home.
greek_mythology.explanation: Arete is the Homeric picture of the wife as functional co-ruler of the household, not an ornament within it.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural, Homer measures a wife's worth by the practical weight she carries in running the house.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: A real and apt figure, but Arete's authority is royal and political rather than the domestic thrift Valluvar specifies.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Xenophon's Oeconomicus, Ischomachus explains that he and his wife are partners in one estate: he brings in from outside, she guards and distributes within, and their joint prosperity depends on her spending in careful proportion to what comes in.
philosophy.explanation: Xenophon's Socratic dialogue is the classical world's fullest treatment of the wife as household economist and co-manager.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the kural's thesis in Greek dress: the wife who matches expenditure to income is the partnership's foundation.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; the indoor/outdoor division of labour and the proportionality principle match the kural very closely.

kurals.tamil:
மனைமாட்சி இல்லாள்கண் இல்லாயின் வாழ்க்கை
எனைமாட்சித் தாயினும் இல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Manaimaatchi illaaLkaN illaayin vaazhkkai,
enaimaatchith thaayinum il.
kurals.meaning: If the wife lacks the excellence that household life requires, then however much splendour a man's life may otherwise possess, it amounts to nothing.
kurals.elementary: A house can have the shiniest roof, the biggest garden and the nicest furniture — but if the roof leaks, none of the rest keeps you dry. This kural says the wife's goodness is the roof: if it's missing, everything else stops counting.
kurals.university: The rhetorical engine here is the word il, which Valluvar uses twice in different senses — il as 'home/household' and il as 'is not, amounts to nothing' — so the couplet ends on the flat negation that domestic splendour without domestic virtue simply is not. Parimelazhagar notes precisely this, glossing the final il as meaning 'useless', not 'absent'. The Tamil didactic tradition amplified the point: the Naaladiyaar declares that a mansion with jewelled lamps but no worthy mistress is 'a cruel forest', an image the anthologist of this chapter explicitly quotes. Comparative scholars often pair this couplet with the near-universal wisdom-literature topos that a household's moral weather is set by the spouse rather than by its wealth — a topos with strikingly parallel formulations in Hebrew Proverbs, Hesiod, and the Pali canon. It should be noted that Valluvar states the principle asymmetrically here; the Kural does address husbandly failure elsewhere (notably Chapter 91, Penvazhich cheral), but this chapter's frame is the wife's contribution.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Mahabharata, Shakuntala reproves King Dushyanta by declaring that the wife is a man's own half and his first friend, the root of dharma, artha and kama and even of liberation, and that the house not occupied by a wife is as desolate as a wilderness however grand it may be.
hinduism.explanation: Shakuntala's speech makes the wife the constitutive element of the household, without which the other goods of life have no ground.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts say the household's splendour collapses into nothing once wifely worth is subtracted.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Sambhava Parva §74 (Shakuntala to Dushyanta; trans. K. M. Ganguli, 1883–96)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Faithful paraphrase of a well-attested passage; marked as paraphrase because Ganguli's exact wording varies between printings.

christianity.quote_or_event: “It is better to dwell in a corner of the housetop, than with a brawling woman in a wide house.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs makes the same trade Valluvar makes: a spacious, splendid house is worth less than a bare corner if the marriage inside it is bad.
christianity.tie_back: Both couplets weigh domestic virtue against domestic magnificence and find the magnificence worthless.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong structural parallel (grandeur vs. character), though Proverbs targets quarrelsomeness specifically rather than the full range of 'manaimaatchi'.

islam.quote_or_event: “The whole world is a provision, and the best object of benefit of the world is the pious woman.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet ranks a righteous wife above every other worldly good a person could possess.
islam.tie_back: Where the Kural says other splendours are worth nothing without her, the hadith says she is worth more than all of them.
islam.source: Sahih Muslim 1467, Book of Suckling, Chapter: Advice with regard to women (narrated by 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr)
islam._accuracy_note: Near-exact inversion of the same claim; wording follows the standard Siddiqui English rendering on sunnah.com.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Rabbi Tanḥum said that Rabbi Ḥanilai said: Any man who does not have a wife is left without joy, without blessing, without goodness.”
judaism.explanation: The Gemara derives from three separate scriptural verses that joy, blessing and goodness all enter a man's life through his wife.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts make the wife the channel through which a household's goods become real goods at all.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Yevamot 62b (Koren Noé / William Davidson Edition)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verbatim from the Davidson translation; speaks of having no wife rather than an unworthy one, which is a slight shift of target.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “When the husband is ethical, bountiful, rid of stinginess, but the wife is unethical, miserly and abusive, she's a zombie living with a god for a husband.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha's four types of marriage make the point that one partner's virtue cannot carry a household whose other partner lacks it.
buddhism.tie_back: Even a wholly virtuous husband's life 'amounts to nothing' as a household when the wife's character is absent.
buddhism.source: Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.53, Paṭhamasaṁvāsa Sutta (trans. Bhikkhu Sujato, SuttaCentral)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verbatim; Sujato's 'zombie' renders Pali chava (corpse). Note the Sutta is symmetrical — it says the same of a bad husband — where the kural is not.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “For a man wins nothing better than a good wife, and, again, nothing worse than a bad one, a greedy soul who roasts her man without fire, strong though he may be, and brings him to a raw old age.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod's farming poem states the good-wife/bad-wife polarity as a maxim of practical life, not as myth.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Almost the identical proposition: no external strength or wealth survives a bad marriage.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 702–705 (trans. H. G. Evelyn-White, Loeb Classical Library, 1914)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Verbatim Loeb text; one of the closest cross-cultural parallels in this chapter.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Between husband and wife friendship seems to exist by nature, for man is naturally disposed to pairing.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle grounds the household not in property or utility alone but in a natural philia between spouses, from which the rest of the household's goods follow.
philosophy.tie_back: If the marital bond itself fails, then on Aristotle's account the household has lost the very thing that made it a household.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Widely attested English rendering, though wording varies across translations (Ross, Rackham, Irwin); Aristotle is explaining marriage's basis rather than diagnosing its failure.

kurals.tamil:
இல்லதென் இல்லவள் மாண்பானால் உள்ளதென்
இல்லவள் மாணாக் கடை.
kurals.transliteration:
Illadhen illavaL maaNbaanaal uLLadhen,
illavaL maaNaak kadai.
kurals.meaning: If the wife of the house is truly excellent, what does a man lack? And if she is not, what does he actually possess?
kurals.elementary: Think of a key. If you have the right key, every locked door in the house opens — so nothing is really shut to you. Lose the key and it doesn't matter how many rooms you own; you can't get into any of them. This kural says a good partner is that key.
kurals.university: The couplet is built as a matched pair of rhetorical questions — illadhu en? ('what is lacking?') against uLLadhu en? ('what is there?') — and the symmetry is the argument: presence and absence of wifely maaNbu are made to exhaust the possibilities, with nothing in between. This antithetical-parallelism structure is a signature of Near Eastern and Tamil wisdom poetry alike, and it produces here a deliberately absolute claim that later Tamil moralists softened or literalised in various directions; Avvaiyar's Moodhurai rewrites it as the image of a house turning into a sour thicket. Parimelazhagar's note that maaNbu, an abstract quality-noun, stands here for the person who has it is an important grammatical observation — Valluvar is not praising an attribute detachable from the woman but identifying her with it. Read together, Kurals 52 and 53 form a diptych: 52 denies that external goods can substitute for her, 53 denies that anything remains once she is subtracted. Comparative scholarship frequently notes that Proverbs 12:4 states the identical antithesis in a single verse, and the Tamil commentarial tradition itself has cited that biblical parallel since at least the nineteenth century.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Offspring, (the due performance of) religious rites, faithful service, highest conjugal happiness and heavenly bliss for the ancestors and oneself, depend on one's wife alone.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu makes the wife the single point on which every major human good — progeny, ritual, pleasure, and even posthumous welfare — is said to rest.
hinduism.tie_back: Exactly the Kural's logic: with her excellence nothing is lacking, without it nothing stands.
hinduism.source: Manusmriti 9.28 (trans. G. Bühler, Sacred Books of the East XXV)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verbatim Bühler text and an unusually precise match — both make the wife the sole condition of a complete life.

christianity.quote_or_event: “A virtuous woman is a crown to her husband: but she that maketh ashamed is as rottenness in his bones.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs poses the same two-sided proposition in a single antithetical verse: the good wife adds everything, the bad one hollows out what is already there.
christianity.tie_back: This is Kural 53's exact structure — the two halves of the couplet matched to the two halves of the verse.
christianity._accuracy_note: Among the closest parallels in the whole chapter; Tamil commentators have themselves cited this verse alongside the kural.

islam.quote_or_event: “And of His signs is that He created for you from yourselves mates that you may find tranquility in them; and He placed between you affection and mercy. Indeed in that are signs for a people who give thought.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an presents a good spouse as a sign of God — the source of sakina (tranquillity), mawadda (affection) and rahma (mercy) in a life.
islam.tie_back: If she supplies these, as the Kural says, there is nothing left for a person to lack.
islam._accuracy_note: Verbatim and thematically strong on the positive half, but the Qur'anic verse has no counterpart to the kural's negative half.

judaism.quote_or_event: Reading the phrase 'a helper against him' (ezer kenegdo) in Genesis, the Talmud teaches that if a man is worthy his wife is his helper, and if he is unworthy she is against him — the same woman functioning as the whole of his fortune or the whole of his misfortune.
judaism.explanation: The rabbinic wordplay turns the ambiguous Hebrew preposition into a doctrine that the marriage is decisive either way.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts make the marriage a binary on which a man's entire condition turns.
judaism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous passage (marked non-quote because English renderings differ widely); the Talmud pivots on the husband's worth rather than the wife's, an inversion worth noting.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Children are the site for human beings. A wife is the best comrade.”
buddhism.explanation: In this short exchange with a deity the Buddha names the wife the supreme companion (paramā sakhā) a person can have.
buddhism.tie_back: If the best of all comrades is secured, as the Kural asks, what is left to lack?
buddhism.source: Saṁyutta Nikāya 1.54, Vatthu Sutta (trans. Bhikkhu Sujato, SuttaCentral)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verbatim; matches the kural's positive half strongly and, as a bonus, pairs wife and children exactly as Kural 60 does.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “For nothing is greater or better than this, when man and wife dwell in a home in one accord, a great grief to their foes and a joy to their friends; but they know it best themselves.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus blesses Nausicaa with homophrosynē — like-mindedness in marriage — which he ranks above every other human good.
greek_mythology.tie_back: 'Nothing greater or better' is Homer's way of saying what the Kural says: with this, nothing is lacking.
greek_mythology.source: Homer, Odyssey 6.182–185 (trans. A. T. Murray, Loeb Classical Library, 1919)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Verbatim Loeb text; Homer's ideal is mutual and symmetrical, whereas the kural is framed around the wife's quality.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Consolation of Philosophy, Boethius — stripped of office, wealth, and freedom and awaiting execution — is reminded by Lady Philosophy that his wife still lives, surpassing all other women in purity of character, and that in her alone he retains a good that outweighs everything fortune has taken.
philosophy.explanation: Boethius's case is the kural's thought-experiment run in reverse: a man who has literally lost everything except a virtuous wife, and is told he is therefore not destitute.
philosophy.tie_back: 'What does he lack?' — Philosophy's answer to Boethius is exactly Valluvar's.
philosophy.source: Boethius, The Consolation of Philosophy, Book II, prose 4 (c. 524 CE)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Accurate paraphrase of a real passage; the argument is about consolation in ruin rather than a general maxim about wives.

kurals.tamil:
பெண்ணின் பெருந்தக்க யாவுள கற்பென்னும்
திண்மைஉண் டாகப் பெறின்.
kurals.transliteration:
PeNNin perundhakka yaavuLa kaRpennum,
thiNmai uNdaagap peRin.
kurals.meaning: If a woman possesses the inner firmness called karpu — steadfast fidelity of mind — what greater treasure is there in the world than she is?
kurals.elementary: Some things are strong because they are heavy, like a rock. Other things are strong because they don't bend, like a steel bar. This kural is about the second kind of strength — the inside kind, where a person decides something and simply never wobbles. It says nothing you could own is worth more than a partner like that.
kurals.university: The pivotal term is thiNmai — hardness, firmness, tensile strength — which Valluvar applies to karpu, and the metaphor is deliberate: karpu is not presented as a restriction imposed from outside but as a structural property of the person, a kalangaa nilaimai (unshakeable state) in Parimelazhagar's phrase. This matters because karpu is one of the most contested words in Tamil literary history: Tolkappiyam already ranks it above naaN (modesty), the Silappatikaram builds its entire tragic architecture on Kannagi's karpu as a force capable of burning a city, and modern Tamil feminist criticism (from Periyarist writing onward) has extensively critiqued the way karpu was later narrowed into a purely sexual and purely female obligation. Valluvar's own usage here is notably psychological rather than juridical — thiNmai is a quality of mind, and the next couplet's imagery of cosmic power flows from it. Comparative readers should note that nearly every tradition surveyed in this chapter has a 'her price is above rubies' formula, but relatively few, like Valluvar, locate the value explicitly in an interior strength rather than in outward conduct or reputation.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Sita, in the Ramayana, is held captive for a year in Ravana's Ashoka grove, offered a queen's throne and threatened with death, and refuses every inducement — her constancy, not her beauty or birth, is what the epic and its commentators treat as her greatness.
hinduism.explanation: Valmiki's Sita became the Indian archetype of pativrata firmness under maximal pressure.
hinduism.tie_back: She is the narrative demonstration of the Kural's claim that this inner firmness is a woman's highest greatness.
hinduism.source: Valmiki, Ramayana, Sundara Kanda (Sita in the Ashoka Vana)
hinduism._accuracy_note: A well-founded archetypal match; the Ramayana also contains the agni-pariksha episode, which modern critics read as undercutting rather than confirming this ideal.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Whose adorning let it not be that outward adorning of plaiting the hair, and of wearing of gold, or of putting on of apparel; But let it be the hidden man of the heart, in that which is not corruptible, even the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit, which is in the sight of God of great price.”
christianity.explanation: 1 Peter explicitly relocates a woman's worth from external ornament to an incorruptible inner disposition described as of 'great price'.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts price an interior, unshakeable quality above anything that can be worn or owned.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong on the inner-strength-over-outward-goods axis; 'meek and quiet' is a different virtue-profile from the Tamil thiNmai (firmness).

islam.quote_or_event: “So righteous women are devoutly obedient, guarding in [the husband's] absence what Allāh would have them guard.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an defines the righteous wife by hifz — self-guarding sustained precisely when no one is watching, which is a form of inner constancy.
islam.tie_back: Guarding what cannot be supervised is what the Kural means by firmness rather than compliance.
islam._accuracy_note: Verbatim excerpt of the relevant clause; readers should note the same verse contains disciplinary provisions that are heavily debated and are not paralleled in the Kural.

judaism.quote_or_event: “A woman of valour who can find? For her price is far above rubies.”
judaism.explanation: Eshet Chayil, the closing acrostic of Proverbs, is sung by many Jewish households to the wife at the Shabbat table every week — a liturgical act of valuation.
judaism.tie_back: 'What greater treasure is there?' is answered identically, and in Judaism the answer is turned into a weekly ritual.
judaism.source: Proverbs 31:10, 'Eshet Chayil' (Jewish Publication Society, 1917); recited in the Friday-night home liturgy
judaism._accuracy_note: Verbatim JPS text and a near-identical rhetorical question; note this verse is shared scripture with Christianity, so the distinctively Jewish element is its liturgical use.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “It's when a lady would not transgress in any way that her husband would not consider agreeable, even for the sake of her own life.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha defines 'acting lovingly toward her husband' as a constancy that would not break even under threat of death.
buddhism.tie_back: This is exactly the thiNmai — firmness that holds when the cost is total — that the Kural calls a woman's greatest worth.
buddhism.source: Aṅguttara Nikāya 8.49, Paṭhamaidhalokika Sutta (trans. Bhikkhu Sujato, SuttaCentral)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verbatim and a genuine match on unbreakable constancy, though framed as conduct toward the husband rather than as intrinsic strength.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Penelope holds the household of Ithaca against 108 suitors for twenty years, unweaving Laertes' shroud each night to buy time, and Homer presents this endurance — not beauty or lineage — as the reason her name became proverbial.
greek_mythology.explanation: The Odyssey's whole plot depends on one woman's refusal to yield, sustained without any external enforcement.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Penelope is the Greek demonstration of the Kural's 'firmness' as a woman's supreme distinction.
greek_mythology.source: Homer, Odyssey, Books 2, 19 and 23 (the shroud, the recognition, the test of the bed)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Very strong archetypal correspondence; Penelope's firmness is also strategic cunning (mētis), a dimension the kural does not name.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the preface to the Bravery of Women, Plutarch argues against Thucydides that courage and the other virtues are one and the same in men and women, differing only in the circumstances that call them out, and offers dozens of historical cases as proof.
philosophy.explanation: Plutarch's essay is antiquity's most sustained philosophical argument that female moral strength is strength in the full sense, not a lesser kind.
philosophy.tie_back: It supplies the philosophical grounding for the Kural's claim that a woman's firmness is the greatest thing there is.
philosophy.source: Plutarch, Mulierum Virtutes (Bravery of Women), Moralia 242E–243A
philosophy._accuracy_note: Genuine and relevant, but Plutarch is arguing about courage in public crises, not the marital constancy the kural means by karpu.

kurals.tamil:
தெய்வம் தொழாஅள் கொழுநன் தொழுதெழுவாள்
பெய்யெனப் பெய்யும் மழை.
kurals.transliteration:
Theyvam thozhaaaL kozhunan thozhudhezhuvaaL,
peyyenap peyyum mazhai.
kurals.meaning: She who worships no other god but reveres her husband as she rises each day — if she says 'rain', the rain will fall.
kurals.elementary: This is a very old saying about how powerful someone's devotion was believed to be: so powerful that even the clouds would listen. People used to tell stories like this to show that a promise kept perfectly gives a person a kind of strength the world has to respect. Today many people read it differently — and disagree with it — which is worth knowing too.
kurals.university: This is the most contested couplet in the chapter and arguably in Book I. Read plainly it asserts that a wife's exclusive devotion to her husband confers thaumaturgic power over nature — a claim with deep roots in Tamil literature, where Kannagi's karpu incinerates Madurai and the chaste woman's word commands the elements. Parimelazhagar reads it straightforwardly as establishing 'the power of the woman of karpu' (kaRpudaiyavaLadhu aatral). But modern readings diverge sharply: M. Karunanidhi's widely circulated commentary renders the couplet critically, treating the woman who worships her husband as god as one who has reduced herself to servitude, while other scholars argue the couplet is hyperbolic praise of moral force rather than a prescription of husband-worship, and still others note that Valluvar's own Chapter 1 pointedly refuses sectarian deity-worship, so 'thozhaaaL theyvam' may be less about theology than about single-pointed commitment. The comparative material below shows that the specific motif — a devoted wife's prayer bringing rain — appears independently in the Babylonian Talmud, which is a remarkable convergence. The honest scholarly position is that the couplet encodes a genuinely asymmetric marital theology that many readers today reject while still finding the underlying claim about the force of integrity intelligible.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Savitri, having chosen the doomed Satyavan and kept a three-day vow, follows Yama as he carries off her husband's soul and argues with the god of death until he returns Satyavan alive — her devotion literally overrides the order of death.
hinduism.explanation: The Mahabharata's most famous pativrata narrative makes wifely devotion a force that even a deity must yield to.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural's claim in narrative form: her constancy commands what no ordinary petition can.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Pativrata-mahatmya Parva (the Savitri and Satyavan episode)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong match on 'devotion commands the cosmos'; Savitri's power works through argument and vow rather than through worshipping her husband as a god.

christianity.quote_or_event: “The effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man availeth much. Elias was a man subject to like passions as we are, and he prayed earnestly that it might not rain: and it rained not on the earth by the space of three years and six months. And he prayed again, and the heaven gave rain.”
christianity.explanation: James offers the New Testament's clearest statement that a sufficiently righteous person's word can govern rainfall.
christianity.tie_back: The same equation as the Kural — perfected righteousness yields command over the rain — though attached to a prophet, not a wife.
christianity._accuracy_note: The rain-at-a-word motif matches exactly, but Christianity has no analogue to the husband-as-sole-object-of-worship premise; scored low for that reason.

islam.quote_or_event: “If I were to order anyone to prostrate to anyone, I would have ordered the woman to prostrate to her husband.”
islam.explanation: The hadith is structured as an emphatic refusal — prostration belongs to God alone — while using the marital bond as the measure of how great a claim the husband has.
islam.tie_back: It sets up the identical tension the Kural does between worship owed to the divine and reverence owed to a spouse.
islam.source: Jami' at-Tirmidhi 1159 (also Sunan Ibn Majah 1852), narrated by Abu Hurayra
islam._accuracy_note: Widely attested wording, though English renderings vary slightly; note the hadith explicitly withholds the act of worship that the kural appears to grant.

judaism.quote_or_event: “They went up to the roof. He stood in one corner and she stood in the other corner. Clouds began to form on that side where his wife stood… Because my wife is frequently at home, and she gives bread to the poor, and therefore her provision of benefit to the needy is immediate.”
judaism.explanation: When the Sages come to the miracle-worker Abba Ḥilkiyya to pray for rain, the clouds gather first over his wife — and he explains that her merit outranks his.
judaism.tie_back: An astonishingly close convergence: a devoted wife whose word brings rain before anyone else's.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Ta'anit 23b (Koren Noé / William Davidson Edition)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verbatim and an unusually exact motif-match on the rain; the Talmud grounds her power in charity to the poor rather than in devotion to her husband.

buddhism.quote_or_event: When the householder Nakulapitā lies gravely ill and fears dying anxious about his family, his wife Nakulamātā speaks to him at length about her own competence and faith, and her words so steady him that his illness subsides — the Buddha later praises her as a teacher in her own right.
buddhism.explanation: Early Buddhism records a wife whose words have transforming power, but locates that power in her wisdom and reassurance, not in veneration of her husband.
buddhism.tie_back: It is the nearest Buddhist analogue to a wife's word achieving what nothing else could, minus the metaphysics.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Deliberately scored low: Buddhism explicitly rejects husband-worship and treats spouses as ethical equals, so this is a best-available 'next-best' match only.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Ceyx drowns at sea, his wife Alcyone throws herself into the waves in grief; the gods transform them both into halcyon birds, and thereafter Aeolus stills the winds and calms the sea for seven days each winter so that she can nest — the 'halcyon days'.
greek_mythology.explanation: Greco-Roman myth's clearest case of the weather itself being ordered to obey the needs of a devoted wife.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Nature bends to a faithful wife, which is precisely the Kural's image of rain falling at her word.
greek_mythology.source: Ovid, Metamorphoses XI.410–748 (the Ceyx and Alcyone episode)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Genuine and apt motif (weather obeys a devoted wife); the transformation is a divine reward after death rather than power wielded in life.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “A wife ought not to make friends of her own, but to enjoy her husband's friends in common with him. The gods are the first and most important friends. Wherefore it is becoming for a wife to worship and to know only the gods that her husband believes in, and to shut the front door tight upon all queer rituals and outlandish superstitions.”
philosophy.explanation: Plutarch's wedding-gift essay advises the bride to adopt her husband's religion exclusively — the same fusion of marital and devotional exclusivity the Kural assumes.
philosophy.tie_back: An almost line-for-line Greco-Roman counterpart to 'she worships no other god'.
philosophy.source: Plutarch, Conjugalia Praecepta (Advice to Bride and Groom) §19, Moralia 140D (trans. F. C. Babbitt, Loeb Classical Library)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verbatim Loeb text and the single closest parallel to this couplet found in any tradition surveyed; both are also open to the same modern critique.

kurals.tamil:
தற்காத்துத் தற்கொண்டாற் பேணித் தகைசான்ற
சொற்காத்துச் சோர்விலாள் பெண்.
kurals.transliteration:
ThaRkaaththuth thaRkoNdaaR peaNith thagaisaandra,
soRkaaththuch soarvilaaL peN.
kurals.meaning: She who guards herself, cherishes the man who married her, keeps the household's good name unblemished, and never slackens in any of it — she is what 'wife' truly means.
kurals.elementary: Think of someone holding three things at once — their own promise, their partner, and the family's good name — and never letting any of the three drop, not even when they're tired. This kural says that's not just a nice thing to do; that's what the word 'wife' actually means.
kurals.university: Structurally this is a definition-by-enumeration, listing four duties and then delivering the predicate in a single final word: peN. Valluvar's three objects of guarding move outward in concentric circles — thaR-kaaththu (guarding the self), thaR-koNdaan peaNi (tending the one who took her), soR-kaaththu (guarding the word, i.e. reputation) — and the fourth term, soarvu-ilaaL ('she in whom there is no slackening'), converts them from acts into a sustained disposition; Parimelazhagar glosses soarvu as maRavi, forgetfulness or lapse, making constancy of attention the operative virtue. The word soL here is usually read by commentators as puhaz, the spoken good name that a village confers, which locates a significant part of wifely virtue in the social rather than the private sphere. Tamil tradition has long linked this couplet to Vasuki Ammaiyar, Valluvar's legendary wife, and the anthologists of this chapter pair it with a line from the deuterocanonical Ben Sira on the doubled days of a good wife's husband. Note also the quiet reciprocity implied: the kural says 'the man who took her' (thaR-koNdaan), keeping the marriage contractual and two-sided even while the duties enumerated are hers.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Mahabharata, Shakuntala tells Dushyanta that the wife is a man's own half and his first friend — a formulation the tradition developed into the terms ardhangini ('half-body') and sahadharmini ('co-bearer of dharma'), making her the joint holder of the household's obligations and its honour.
hinduism.explanation: The sahadharmini concept makes protection of the husband and of the family's dharmic standing the wife's own duty, not a service rendered.
hinduism.tie_back: Both traditions make guarding the husband and the household's name part of the definition of wifehood itself.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Adi Parva §74; the ardhangini / sahadharmini formulations in classical dharma literature
hinduism._accuracy_note: Sound paraphrase of a well-attested passage and concept; the Sanskrit terms are later crystallisations rather than words in the epic line itself.

christianity.quote_or_event: “The heart of her husband doth safely trust in her, so that he shall have no need of spoil. She will do him good and not evil all the days of her life… She looketh well to the ways of her household, and eateth not the bread of idleness.”
christianity.explanation: The Proverbs 31 wife is defined by unwearying diligence sustained 'all the days of her life' — the exact opposite of soarvu, slackening.
christianity.tie_back: 'Never slackens' and 'eateth not the bread of idleness' are the same virtue named in two languages.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verbatim; covers guarding the husband's interests, the household, and tireless constancy — three of the kural's four terms.

islam.quote_or_event: “They are clothing for you and you are clothing for them.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'anic libās metaphor makes each spouse the other's covering — protection, warmth, and the preservation of the other's honour from exposure.
islam.tie_back: Guarding oneself, one's spouse, and the couple's good name is exactly what 'being each other's clothing' means.
islam._accuracy_note: Verbatim and a rich image for mutual guarding, but the Qur'anic clause is symmetrical where the kural assigns the duties to the wife.

judaism.quote_or_event: “One who loves his wife as he loves himself, and who honors her more than himself, and who instructs his sons and daughters in an upright path… about him the verse states: And you shall know that your tent is in peace.”
judaism.explanation: The Talmudic baraita defines the well-ordered household by a standard of unremitting mutual honour rather than by wealth.
judaism.tie_back: The same picture of a marriage held together by sustained, deliberate care for the other's standing.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Yevamot 62b (Koren Noé / William Davidson Edition)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verbatim, and a genuine parallel on guarding the spouse's honour — but the Talmud here addresses the husband's duty, mirroring rather than matching the kural.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Samajīvina Sutta the Buddha tells Nakulapitā and Nakulamātā that a couple who wish to be together in this life and the next should be matched in faith, ethics, generosity and wisdom — a marriage sustained by both partners' unslackening practice rather than by one partner's effort.
buddhism.explanation: Early Buddhism frames marital constancy as a jointly maintained discipline with a definite ethical content.
buddhism.tie_back: The same insistence that wifely (and husbandly) virtue is a continuous practice, not an occasional act.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Accurate summary of a well-known sutta; strictly symmetrical between spouses, which the kural is not.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Therefore the fame of her virtue shall never perish, but the immortals shall make among men on earth a pleasant song in honor of constant Penelope.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Agamemnon's ghost praises Penelope for having guarded both herself and her absent husband's name for twenty years — and says the gods will reward that guardianship with permanent renown.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Guarding the good name (soR-kaappu) is precisely what Homer says wins Penelope her immortal song.
greek_mythology.source: Homer, Odyssey 24.196–198 (trans. A. T. Murray, Loeb Classical Library, 1919)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Verbatim Loeb text; maps onto three of the kural's four clauses (guarding self, husband, reputation) with striking exactness.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “But in marriage there must be above all perfect companionship and mutual love of husband and wife, both in health and in sickness and under all conditions, since it was with desire for this as well as for having children that both entered upon marriage.”
philosophy.explanation: Musonius Rufus, the Roman Stoic, defines marriage by a companionship that must hold 'under all conditions' — a formal refusal of slackening.
philosophy.tie_back: 'Never slackens' is Valluvar's phrase for what Musonius calls constancy in health and in sickness and under all conditions.
philosophy.source: Musonius Rufus, Fragment XIII A, 'On the Chief End of Marriage' (trans. Cora E. Lutz, Yale Classical Studies X, 1947)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verbatim Lutz translation; Musonius applies the standard equally to both spouses, which is a real and significant difference from the kural.

kurals.tamil:
சிறைகாக்கும் காப்பெவன் செய்யும் மகளிர்
நிறைகாக்கும் காப்பே தலை.
kurals.transliteration:
SiRaikaakkum kaappevan seyyum magaLir,
niRaikaakkum kaappe thalai.
kurals.meaning: What can confinement and surveillance ever accomplish? The only guard worth having is the guard women keep over themselves through their own inner steadiness.
kurals.elementary: You can't make a plant grow by building a cage around it — the growing happens inside the plant or it doesn't happen at all. This kural says the same about being good: locking someone up doesn't make them trustworthy. Only the choice they make inside themselves does.
kurals.university: This couplet is one of the strongest statements of moral autonomy anywhere in ancient world literature, and its force depends on a precise contrast between two words for 'guarding': siRai (an enclosure — the word covers a dam, a fortress wall, a prison) and niRai (fullness, the mind held steady in its own course). Parimelazhagar spells out the mechanism — siRai means walls and gatekeepers, niRai means 'setting the heart firm in the way of karpu' — and concludes that without the latter the former produces nothing, which is why Valluvar writes kaappe with the exclusive particle. The couplet is frequently cited in modern Tamil discourse as evidence that Valluvar opposed the seclusion of women, and it is genuinely difficult to read otherwise: the opening is a rhetorical question with a contemptuous edge (evan seyyum — 'what will it do?'). It is also a remarkable convergence with Manusmriti 9.12, which makes the same argument in almost the same words, suggesting a shared ancient Indic debate about the futility of physical guardianship. The obvious limitation, which honest scholarship should name, is that Valluvar's alternative to confinement is internalised self-restraint rather than freedom as such; the couplet dismantles the prison without dismantling the expectation.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Women confined in the house under trusted servants are not well guarded; really well guarded are those who guard themselves by themselves.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu makes the identical argument — external custody fails, self-custody succeeds — using the same confinement-versus-self-guarding contrast.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural's proposition almost word for word, in a different language and legal tradition.
hinduism.source: Manusmriti 9.12 (trans. Ganganath Jha, with Medhātithi's commentary, 1920)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verbatim and the single closest textual parallel in this chapter; both texts share the confinement/self-guarding antithesis exactly.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Keep thy heart with all diligence; for out of it are the issues of life.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs locates the decisive act of guarding in the heart, on the grounds that every outward act originates there — so guarding anything else is guarding downstream.
christianity.tie_back: Same principle: the only guard that matters is the one kept over the inner life.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verbatim and a strong match on inner-vs-outer guarding, though it is addressed to everyone rather than framed against the confinement of women.

islam.quote_or_event: “Tell the believing men to reduce [some] of their vision and guard their private parts… And tell the believing women to reduce [some] of their vision and guard their private parts.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an addresses the command to self-restraint to men first and then to women, framing modesty as a personal discipline rather than something enforced by custody.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, the operative verb is 'guard yourselves' — the responsibility is interior and reciprocal, not imposed by walls.
islam._accuracy_note: Verbatim excerpt; the self-guarding framing matches well, though the passage prescribes outward norms that the kural does not.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Who is mighty? He who subdues his evil inclination, as it is said: 'He who is slow to anger is better than the mighty, and he who rules over his spirit than he who conquers a city.'”
judaism.explanation: Ben Zoma redefines strength as self-mastery and explicitly rates it above the capture of a walled city — the very image of external containment.
judaism.tie_back: The Mishnah's 'ruling one's own spirit beats taking a fortress' is the Kural's siRai/niRai contrast in another key.
judaism._accuracy_note: Well-attested wording and a genuine self-mastery-over-fortification parallel, but it is a general ethical maxim with no reference to women or marriage.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Oneself, indeed, is one's own protector. Who else could the protector be?”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada's Atta Vagga makes self-guardianship not merely the best option but the only real one.
buddhism.tie_back: 'What can confinement accomplish?' and 'who else could the protector be?' are the same rhetorical question.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verbatim Buddharakkhita rendering and an exceptionally close structural match on self-protection as primary.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: King Acrisius, warned that his daughter's son would kill him, shuts Danaë inside a sealed bronze chamber underground — and Zeus reaches her anyway as a shower of golden rain, so that Perseus is born and the prophecy is fulfilled exactly as if the chamber had never existed.
greek_mythology.explanation: Greek myth's definitive demonstration that architectural confinement of a woman achieves nothing whatsoever.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Danaë's bronze room is the Kural's siRai — the guard that does not work.
greek_mythology.source: Apollodorus, The Library 2.4.1; Pindar, Pythian 12; Horace, Odes 3.16
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: An apt and vivid illustration of the futility of confinement, though the myth turns on divine power rather than on the woman's own moral agency.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle argues that acts done under compulsion are not voluntary and therefore not subject to praise or blame at all, and that moral virtue is formed only by repeated chosen action — which means enforced behaviour, however correct, cannot constitute character.
philosophy.explanation: The Nicomachean Ethics supplies the formal reason the Kural's siRai fails: coerced conduct is by definition not virtue.
philosophy.tie_back: Valluvar's 'what will confinement do?' has its philosophical answer here — it can produce compliance but never niRai.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics II.1 (1103a–b) and III.1 (1109b–1110a)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Accurate summary of Aristotle's doctrine of the voluntary and of habituation; Aristotle is not discussing women or marriage, so the application is ours.

kurals.tamil:
பெற்றாற் பெறின்பெறுவர் பெண்டிர் பெருஞ்சிறப்புப்
புத்தேளிர் வாழும் உலகு.
kurals.transliteration:
PetraaR peRin peRuvar peNdir perunjiRappup,
puththeLir vaazhum ulagu.
kurals.meaning: Women who faithfully honour the husband they have received will obtain great glory in the world where the celestials dwell.
kurals.elementary: This kural is about a reward that doesn't come in this life. It says that quietly doing right by your family, day after day, with nobody applauding, is the kind of thing that gets remembered in the highest place there is — even if nobody on earth noticed.
kurals.university: The couplet is a masterclass in Tamil sound-patterning — petraaR peRin peRuvar peNdir perunjiRappu stacks five p-initial words in a single line — and Valluvar uses the alliterative momentum to carry the chapter from the domestic to the cosmic register. Parimelazhagar supplies the elided verb (vazhipaduthal, 'reverencing'), giving the standard reading: women who honour their husbands are themselves honoured by the puttheLir (devas). But the couplet is genuinely ambiguous in Tamil, and the divergence in the commentaries is instructive: M. Varadarajan reads it as the wife's reward for duty, while M. Karunanidhi reads petraaR as 'a husband of good character whom she obtains', making the couplet about a woman's good fortune in her marriage rather than her merit in it. Either way, the structural function is clear — after four couplets defining the wife's excellence, Valluvar extends its consequence past death, a move he makes sparingly in the Aram book. The comparative material below is unusually rich here, because nearly every tradition surveyed developed an explicit doctrine of otherworldly recompense for the faithful wife, and several of them (Manu, the Talmud, the Pali canon) specify the heavenly destination with the same concreteness Valluvar does.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “She who, controlling her thoughts, words, and deeds, never slights her lord, resides (after death) with her husband (in heaven), and is called a virtuous (wife).”
hinduism.explanation: Manu promises a specific post-mortem destination — continued union in heaven — as the reward for the wife's fidelity.
hinduism.tie_back: The same promise the Kural makes: honour the husband here, obtain glory in the world of the celestials.
hinduism.source: Manusmriti 5.165 (trans. G. Bühler, Sacred Books of the East XXV)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verbatim Bühler text and an almost exact doctrinal match on heavenly reward for wifely devotion.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Likewise, ye husbands, dwell with them according to knowledge, giving honour unto the wife, as unto the weaker vessel, and as being heirs together of the grace of life; that your prayers be not hindered.”
christianity.explanation: 1 Peter assigns husband and wife a shared inheritance in the life to come, making the wife a full heir of grace rather than a dependent beneficiary.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts extend the wife's standing from the household into the world beyond it.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verbatim; 'heirs together of the grace of life' matches the heavenly-glory theme well, though the verse addresses husbands and contains the much-debated 'weaker vessel' phrase.

islam.quote_or_event: “If a woman prays her five daily prayers, fasts her month, guards her chastity and obeys her husband, it will be said to her: Enter Paradise by whichever of the gates of Paradise you wish.”
islam.explanation: The hadith names four conditions — three of them acts of worship, the fourth marital — and attaches to them an unrestricted entry to Paradise.
islam.tie_back: Precisely the Kural's structure: fidelity in marriage counted among the things that win 'great glory' in the world of the celestials.
islam.source: Hadith of the Prophet Muhammad, Musnad Ahmad 1661 and Ibn Hibban 4163; also Mishkat al-Masabih 3254 (graded hasan)
islam._accuracy_note: Wording is the standard English rendering; note that this hadith's numbering varies across collections and it is not in Bukhari or Muslim.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Greater is the promise for the future made by the Holy One, Blessed be He, to women than to men… Rav said to Rabbi Ḥiyya: By what virtue do women merit to receive this reward? Rabbi Ḥiyya answered: They merit this reward for bringing their children to read the Torah in the synagogue, and for sending their husbands to study mishna in the study hall, and for waiting for their husbands until they return from the study hall.”
judaism.explanation: The Gemara asks directly how women earn the World to Come and answers entirely in terms of what they enable for husband and children.
judaism.tie_back: Same claim, same structure: domestic faithfulness converted into an outsized share of heavenly reward.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 17a (Koren Noé / William Davidson Edition)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verbatim from the Davidson translation and a remarkably direct parallel, including the promise that women's reward exceeds men's.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Accomplished in sixteen respects, complete with the eight factors, a virtuous laywoman such as she is reborn in the realm of the Agreeable Gods.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha tells Visākhā that the laywoman who fulfils the four this-worldly and four next-worldly qualities is reborn among the manāpakāyika devas.
buddhism.tie_back: The Pali text names the same destination the Kural does — the world where the celestials dwell.
buddhism.source: Aṅguttara Nikāya 8.49, Paṭhamaidhalokika Sutta (trans. Bhikkhu Sujato, SuttaCentral)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verbatim; the deva-realm reward for a virtuous wife is a direct match, though the sutta's causes include faith and wisdom alongside marital conduct.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Alcestis volunteers to die in her husband Admetus's place when no one else will; Euripides' play has the house honour her as a blessed spirit and the chorus promise her a hymn among the living, before Heracles wrestles Death and brings her back.
greek_mythology.explanation: Greek tragedy's clearest case of a wife's devotion earning her a status beyond ordinary mortality.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Alcestis receives exactly what the Kural promises — great glory beyond the grave for an act of marital fidelity.
greek_mythology.source: Euripides, Alcestis (438 BCE), esp. lines 435–475 and 1000–1005
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong archetypal match on posthumous honour for a devoted wife; Euripides is also widely read as ironising Admetus, which complicates the moral.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Phaedrus, Socrates describes souls who live together with self-mastery rather than surrender to appetite: they win a bright and blessed life, and when their time ends they grow their wings together and rise, having begun the same ascent side by side.
philosophy.explanation: Plato gives a philosophical rather than devotional version of the promise — shared moral discipline in a bonded pair converts into a shared ascent.
philosophy.tie_back: Both texts end a description of earthly fidelity with a claim about what the faithful receive in the world above.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Genuine on the 'shared discipline yields shared heavenly reward' axis, but Plato's pairs are philosophical lovers, not spouses, and the context is pederastic erōs.

kurals.tamil:
புகழ்புரிந்த இல்லிலோர்க்கு இல்லை இகழ்வார்முன்
ஏறுபோல் பீடு நடை.
kurals.transliteration:
Pugazhpurindha illiloarkku illai igazhvaarmun,
ERupoal peedu nadai.
kurals.meaning: A man whose wife does not care for the household's good name cannot walk with the proud, lion-like stride before those who hold him in contempt.
kurals.elementary: Imagine walking into a room where people are whispering about you. If you know you've done nothing wrong at home, you can walk in with your head up. If you know you have, your feet get heavy. This kural says a family's good name is what lets someone stand tall in front of people who don't like them.
kurals.university: Valluvar shifts register here from the household's interior to its public face, and the image he chooses — ERu, the bull or male lion, with peedu nadai, a gait of dignified swagger — is drawn from the heroic vocabulary of Sangam puRam poetry, where such a walk signals a warrior's untouchable standing. Parimelazhagar reads the couplet as stating the specific defect that follows when the soR-kaappu of Kural 56 is neglected, which makes 55–59 a tightly argued sequence rather than a list. The sociology behind it is worth naming: in the honour economy of ancient Tamil society, a household's puhaz was a collective asset that any member could deplete, so Valluvar's claim is descriptive as much as normative — the man's public bearing is materially constituted by his wife's reputation. Modern readers rightly note the asymmetry (the wife's conduct determines the husband's honour, but the couplet says nothing of the reverse) and the fact that this logic is precisely what later hardened into honour-based control of women; it is worth setting beside Kural 57, where Valluvar explicitly rejects control as a method. Comparative wisdom literature converges here almost uncannily: Proverbs 31:23, Bava Metzia 59a, and Odyssey 11 all tie a man's standing in the public assembly directly to his wife.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Where women are honoured, there the gods are pleased; but where they are not honoured, no sacred rite yields rewards.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu ties the standing and efficacy of an entire household — even its ritual power — to how its women are treated and how they fare.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts make a family's public and sacred standing contingent on the honour surrounding its women.
hinduism.source: Manusmriti 3.56 (trans. G. Bühler, Sacred Books of the East XXV)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Widely quoted Bühler rendering; the causal arrow runs the opposite way (how women are honoured, rather than how they guard honour), so it is a mirror rather than a match.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Her husband is known in the gates, when he sitteth among the elders of the land.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs places the excellent wife's effect precisely where the Kural does — at the city gate, the public forum where a man's standing is measured.
christianity.tie_back: The same proposition: a wife's worth is what lets a man hold his place among his peers.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verbatim, and one of the sharpest matches in the chapter — both locate the payoff in public standing rather than private happiness.

islam.quote_or_event: “The best of you are those who are best to their wives, and I am the best of you to my wives.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet makes the treatment of one's wife the public measure of a man's rank among men, and offers himself as the standard.
islam.tie_back: Both sayings make a man's standing before others a function of his marriage.
islam.source: Jami' at-Tirmidhi 3895 (also Sunan Ibn Majah 1977), narrated by 'A'isha
islam._accuracy_note: Widely attested wording, but it measures the husband by his conduct toward his wife, whereas the kural measures him by hers — a reversal worth flagging.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And Rabbi Ḥelbo says: A person must always be careful about sustaining the honor of his wife, as blessing is found in a person's house only because of his wife… And that is what Rava said to the residents of Meḥoza: Honor your wives, so that you will become rich.”
judaism.explanation: The Gemara makes a household's prosperity and honour flow through the wife, and turns that into a practical instruction to the men of the town.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts say a man's visible fortunes stand or fall with his wife's honour.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Bava Metzia 59a (Koren Noé / William Davidson Edition)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verbatim from the Davidson translation; the Talmud places the obligation on the husband to honour her, where the kural places it on her to guard the name.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Bhariya Sutta the Buddha describes seven kinds of wife — three of them 'like a murderer', 'like a thief' and 'like a tyrant', who bring their households to ruin and themselves to a bad destination, and four (like a mother, a sister, a friend, a servant) who bring the household to flourishing.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha tells Sujata that these types differ not in wealth or status but in the reputation and outcome they produce for the whole house.
buddhism.tie_back: The kural's negative case — the household whose name the wife does not guard — is the Bhariya Sutta's first three types exactly.
buddhism.source: Aṅguttara Nikāya 7.63, Bhariya Sutta (the Buddha to Sujātā, in Anāthapiṇḍika's house)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Accurate summary of a well-known sutta; it is directed at the wife's own destination more than at the husband's public bearing.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Agamemnon returns from Troy as the greatest conqueror of his age and is murdered in his bath by Clytemnestra; his shade tells Odysseus in the underworld that she poured shame on herself and on all women to come, so that even a good wife now inherits the ill report she created.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer's most powerful illustration that no quantity of public glory survives a household's disgrace.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Agamemnon is the man who cannot walk with the lion's stride, however many cities he sacked.
greek_mythology.source: Homer, Odyssey 11.405–434 (the shade of Agamemnon to Odysseus)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Very strong narrative match on public glory annulled by domestic dishonour; paraphrased rather than quoted because the relevant lines span a long speech.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle's portrait of the megalopsychos — the great-souled man — includes his outward bearing: a deep voice, a level speech, an unhurried gait, because he holds few things in high enough esteem to be hurried by them; yet Aristotle also insists that greatness of soul cannot be sustained without the external goods that give a claim to honour.
philosophy.explanation: The Nicomachean Ethics both describes the proud walk the Kural names and explains why it cannot be bluffed when the grounds for honour are missing.
philosophy.tie_back: Valluvar's lion-stride is Aristotle's megalopsychos gait — and both make it depend on having real standing to walk on.
philosophy._accuracy_note: A real and interesting parallel on bearing-as-index-of-honour, but Aristotle never connects it to a spouse; the link is interpretive.

kurals.tamil:
மங்கலம் என்ப மனைமாட்சி மற்று அதன்
நன்கலம் நன்மக்கட் பேறு.
kurals.transliteration:
Mangalam enba manaimaatchi matru adhan,
nankalam nanmakkat peRu.
kurals.meaning: The wise say that the wife's excellence is the true auspiciousness of a home; and that good children are the fine jewel with which that auspiciousness is adorned.
kurals.elementary: A birthday cake is the good part. The candles on top make it look even better — but they're not the cake. This kural says the wife's goodness is the cake and good children are the candles: lovely, but only because there's something underneath to put them on.
kurals.university: The couplet closes the chapter on a two-term metaphor of extraordinary economy: manaimaatchi is mangalam (the auspicious thing itself, the blessing), and children are its nan-kalam (its good ornament) — and the near-pun between mangalam and nankalam binds the two halves phonetically while separating them logically. The hierarchy matters: an ornament presupposes something to adorn, so Valluvar is explicitly subordinating progeny to character, a striking priority in a culture where sons carried ritual obligations for the ancestors. Parimelazhagar supplies the unstated subject — enba, 'so the knowing say' — and observes that the couplet functions as a thoRRuvaay, a doorway opening onto Chapter 7 (Makkat-peRu), so that the chapter's last word is also the next chapter's first subject. The comparative field here is unusually convergent, since almost every tradition pairs a virtuous wife with flourishing children as a single image of blessing: Psalm 128 does it with a vine and olive shoots, the Qur'an with 'comfort of the eyes', and the Pali Maṅgala Sutta — which shares the very word maṅgala with the Tamil mangalam through their common Indic root — lists care for partner and children among the highest blessings.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Rig Veda's marriage hymn blesses the bride as she enters her husband's house, asking that she rule there with authority, that the household prosper, and that she be the mother of living heroes — placing the wife's standing first and children as the blessing that flows from it.
hinduism.explanation: The oldest Indic wedding liturgy already frames the bride's establishment in the home and the children who follow as one continuous benediction.
hinduism.tie_back: The same ordering as the Kural: the wife is the blessing, the children are its adornment.
hinduism.source: Rig Veda 10.85 (the Sūryā-vivāha / marriage hymn), esp. vv. 42–47 (trans. R. T. H. Griffith, 1896)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Faithful summary of the hymn's blessings; paraphrased because the hymn's benedictions are distributed across many verses rather than stated in one line.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Thy wife shall be as a fruitful vine by the sides of thine house: thy children like olive plants round about thy table.”
christianity.explanation: The psalm pictures the blessed household as one image with two elements — the wife at its centre and the children ranged around her.
christianity.tie_back: Identical pairing and identical priority: the wife is the vine, the children are what grows around her.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verbatim and an exceptionally close match — the same two-term picture of domestic blessing in the same order.

islam.quote_or_event: “And those who say, 'Our Lord, grant us from among our wives and offspring comfort to our eyes and make us a leader [i.e., example] for the righteous.'”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an's portrait of the servants of the Most Merciful culminates in a prayer that names wives and offspring together as the qurrat a'yun — the coolness of the eyes.
islam.tie_back: The same closing gesture: wife and good children named as a single blessing on the household.
islam._accuracy_note: Verbatim; pairs spouse and children as one blessing exactly as the kural does, though without the ornament/ornamented hierarchy.

judaism.quote_or_event: Rav Huna teaches that one who is habitually careful with the Sabbath lamp will have sons who are Torah scholars — the household's light, kindled by the wife as a domestic religious act, being treated as the direct cause of the children's distinction.
judaism.explanation: The Talmud makes the wife's faithful keeping of the home's central ritual the thing that produces children worth having.
judaism.tie_back: Same causal order: the wife's household excellence is the blessing, and good children are what that blessing yields.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 23b (Rav Huna on the Shabbat lamp)
judaism._accuracy_note: Accurate paraphrase of a well-known passage; 'lamp' is literal in the Talmud and metaphorical in the kural, so the correspondence is thematic.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Caring for mother and father, kindness to children and partners, and unstressful work: this is the highest blessing.”
buddhism.explanation: The Maṅgala Sutta is the Buddha's canonical answer to the question of what the highest blessings are, and household relationships are among them.
buddhism.tie_back: The Tamil mangalam and the Pali maṅgala are the same word, and both couplets answer the same question: what actually blesses a home?
buddhism.source: Sutta Nipāta 2.4, Maṅgala Sutta (trans. Bhikkhu Sujato, SuttaCentral)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verbatim, and the shared Indic term maṅgala makes this a genuine lexical as well as thematic parallel.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Baucis and Philemon, poor and long married, unknowingly host Jupiter and Mercury and give them everything they have; the gods spare their cottage from the flood, turn it into a temple, and grant the couple's only wish — to serve there together and to die in the same hour, whereupon they become two intertwined trees.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid's tale is the classical world's fullest picture of a marriage that is itself the blessing on a house, transforming the house into a sacred place.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The household made auspicious by the quality of the marriage within it — the Kural's mangalam in Latin verse.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Honest low score: the marriage-as-blessing-on-the-house theme is a real match, but Baucis and Philemon are childless, so the kural's second half has no counterpart.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “For since the reproductive instinct is by Nature's gift the common possession of all living creatures, the first bond of union is that between husband and wife; the next, that between parents and children; then we find one home, with everything in common.”
philosophy.explanation: Cicero builds society outward from the marriage bond, with the parent–child bond as the second term and the shared household as their joint product.
philosophy.tie_back: Exactly the Kural's ordering — the marriage first, the children next, and the blessed home as what the two together constitute.
philosophy.source: Cicero, De Officiis I.17.54 (trans. Walter Miller, Loeb Classical Library, 1913)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verbatim Loeb text; the sequence marriage → children → shared home mirrors the kural's blessing → ornament → household with real precision.
